s.line: Even with eyes protected by the green spectacles, Dorothy and her friends were at first dazzled by the brilliancy of the wonderful City.
s.note: מוּגָן (protected) is a hof'al participle, the passive of hif'il הֵגֵן (to protect): הֵגֵן עַל = to defend. The same root gives מָגֵן (shield), as in מָגֵן דָּוִד. הִסְתַּנְוֵר = to be dazzled, from סִנְוֵר (to blind with light), used of headlights: הָאוֹרוֹת סִנְוְרוּ אוֹתִי.

s.line: The streets were lined with beautiful houses all built of green marble and studded everywhere with sparkling emeralds.
s.note: מְשֻׁבָּץ (set, studded) is a pu'al participle of שִׁבֵּץ (to set in place). Today שִׁבֵּץ mostly means "to assign, slot in": שִׁבְּצוּ אוֹתִי בַּמִּשְׁמֶרֶת שֶׁל הַלַּיְלָה (they put me on the night shift). A checked pattern is מְשֻׁבָּץ too, and מִשְׁבְּצוֹת are the squares on a chessboard.

s.line: They walked over a pavement of the same green marble,
and where the blocks were joined together were rows of emeralds, set closely, and glittering in the brightness of the sun.
s.note: חֻבַּר (was joined) is pu'al, the passive of pi'el חִבֵּר (to join, connect; also "to add" in arithmetic). זֶה לָזֶה / זוֹ לָזוֹ = "to each other", masculine and feminine: אֶבֶן is feminine, אִזְמָרַגְד masculine.

s.line: The window panes were of green glass;
s.note: שִׁמְשָׁה (windowpane) comes from the same root as שֶׁמֶשׁ. The car's windshield is הַשִּׁמְשָׁה הַקִּדְמִית.

s.line: even the sky above the City had a green tint, and the rays of the sun were green.
s.note: קֶרֶן = a ray (plural קַרְנַיִם, feminine, so יְרֻקּוֹת). The same word means a horn and, in finance, a fund: קֶרֶן פֶּנְסְיָה (pension fund).

s.line: There were many people—men, women, and children—walking about,
s.note: הִסְתּוֹבֵב = to wander around, and also "to turn around". You'll hear סְתָם הִסְתּוֹבַבְתִּי בָּעִיר = I was just hanging around town.

w: וְהָיָה לָהֶם|and they had|~lit. there was to them
s.line: and these were all dressed in green clothes and had greenish skins.
s.note: יְרַקְרַק = greenish. Repeating the last two root letters softens a colour: אֲדַמְדַּם (reddish), לְבַנְבַּן (whitish), שְׁחַרְחַר (darkish).

s.line: They looked at Dorothy and her strangely assorted company with wondering eyes,
and the children all ran away and hid behind their mothers when they saw the Lion;
s.note: הִתְחַבֵּא (hitpa'el) = to hide oneself; הֶחְבִּיא (hif'il) = to hide something. Children play מַחְבּוֹאִים, hide-and-seek, from the same root.

s.line: but no one spoke to them.
Many shops stood in the street, and Dorothy saw that everything in them was green.
Green candy and green pop-corn were offered for sale, as well as green shoes, green hats, and green clothes of all sorts.
s.note: מָכְרוּ with no subject = "were sold", the impersonal plural from chapter 1. Watch the adjective endings: נַעֲלַיִם is feminine (יְרֻקּוֹת), כּוֹבָעִים and בְּגָדִים masculine (יְרֻקִּים).

s.line: At one place a man was selling green lemonade,
and when the children bought it Dorothy could see that they paid for it with green pennies.
s.note: מַטְבֵּעַ (coin; also "currency": מַטְבֵּעַ חוּץ = foreign currency) is masculine even though its plural is מַטְבְּעוֹת, so the adjective is יְרֻקִּים. שִׁלֵּם (pi'el) = to pay; שִׁלֵּם עַל = to pay for.

s.line: There seemed to be no horses nor animals of any kind;
s.note: בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים = animals (singular בַּעַל חַיִּים), the בַּעַל + noun pattern you know. חַיָּה is more "wild beast"; a pet is חַיַּת מַחְמָד.

s.line: the men carried things around in little green carts, which they pushed before them.
s.note: הִסִּיעַ (hif'il) = to drive or carry someone or something; נָסַע (pa'al) = to travel. אֲנִי אַסִּיעַ אוֹתְךָ = I'll give you a lift. A supermarket trolley is עֲגָלָה too.

s.line: Everyone seemed happy and contented and prosperous.
s.note: מְרֻצֶּה (satisfied) is a pu'al participle like מְאֻשָּׁר: אֲנִי מְרֻצֶּה מֵהַתּוֹצָאוֹת = I'm pleased with the results. מְשַׂגְשֵׂג (thriving, prospering) is a news word: כַּלְכָּלָה מְשַׂגְשֶׂגֶת = a booming economy.

w: שׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|the Guardian of the Gates
s.line: The Guardian of the Gates led them through the streets until they came to a big building, exactly in the middle of the City,
which was the Palace of Oz, the Great Wizard.

w: וְהָיָה לוֹ|and he had|~lit. there was to him
s.line: There was a soldier before the door, dressed in a green uniform and wearing a long green beard.
s.note: מַדִּים = uniform, always plural: לוֹבֵשׁ מַדִּים = in uniform, i.e. serving in the army. Without vowels זקן is both זָקָן (beard) and זָקֵן (old man); context decides.

w: שׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|the Guardian of the Gates
s.line: “Here are strangers,” said the Guardian of the Gates to him, “and they demand to see the Great Oz.”
s.note: דָּרַשׁ = to demand. Its pa'ul participle דָּרוּשׁ means "needed, wanted", the word at the top of job ads: דְּרוּשִׁים עוֹבְדִים (workers wanted).

s.line: “Step inside,” answered the soldier, “and I will carry your message to him.”
s.note: מָסַר = to hand over or pass on: תִּמְסֹר לָהּ דְּרִישַׁת שָׁלוֹם = give her my regards. הִכָּנְסוּ is the plural imperative of nif'al נִכְנַס.

s.line: So they passed through the Palace Gates and were led into a big room with a green carpet and lovely green furniture set with emeralds.
s.note: הוּבְלוּ (were led) is hof'al, the passive of hif'il הוֹבִיל (led) from the first sentence of this paragraph. The pair hif'il הוֹ־ / hof'al הוּ־ is regular: הוֹדִיעַ announced → הוּדַע was announced.

s.line: The soldier made them all wipe their feet upon a green mat before entering this room,
s.note: הִכְרִיחַ + infinitive = to force or make someone do something; מֻכְרָח (hof'al) = forced, "have to": אֲנִי מֻכְרָח לָלֶכֶת. שְׁטִיחוֹן is שָׁטִיחַ + the diminutive ending ־וֹן.

s.line: and when they were seated he said politely:

w: תַּרְגִּישׁוּ בְּנוֹחַ|make yourselves comfortable|~lit. you will feel comfortable
s.line: “Please make yourselves comfortable while I go to the door of the Throne Room and tell Oz you are here.”
s.note: תַּרְגִּישׁוּ בְּנוֹחַ: a future verb used as a polite request, the normal way to ask in spoken Hebrew. כֵּס is a throne, a higher word than כִּסֵּא (chair); כֵּס הַמַּלְכוּת = the royal throne.

s.line: They had to wait a long time before the soldier returned.
s.note: נֶאֱלַץ = "had to", literally "was forced": the nif'al passive of pi'el אִלֵּץ (to compel). It is a bit stronger than הָיָה צָרִיךְ: נֶאֱלַצְנוּ לְבַטֵּל = we were forced to cancel.

s.line: When, at last, he came back, Dorothy asked:
“Have you seen Oz?”
s.note: A yes/no question in Hebrew is just a statement with a rising voice: <t>רָאִיתָ אֶת אוֹז</t> = "you saw Oz" or "did you see Oz?". There is no separate perfect tense, so the simple past covers "have you seen".

s.line: “Oh, no,” returned the soldier; “I have never seen him.
But I spoke to him as he sat behind his screen and gave him your message.
s.note: פַּרְגּוֹד = a screen in the sense of a partition or curtain. A TV or computer screen is a different word, מָסָךְ.

s.line: He said he will grant you an audience, if you so desire;
s.note: קִבֵּל אֶת a person = to receive them, give them an audience. A doctor's or clerk's office hours are קַבָּלַת קָהָל ("receiving the public"). Hebrew reported speech keeps the original tense: אָמַר שֶׁהוּא יְקַבֵּל = "said he will receive".

s.line: but each one of you must enter his presence alone,
and he will admit but one each day.
Therefore, as you must remain in the Palace for several days, I will have you shown to rooms where you may rest in comfort after your journey.”
s.note: דָּאַג שֶׁ… = to make sure that …, "see to it": אֲנִי אֶדְאַג לְזֶה = I'll take care of it. On its own דָּאַג = to worry, and דָּאַג לְ… = to look after someone. תִּצְטָרְכוּ is the hitpa'el of צָרִיךְ: הִצְטָרֵךְ = to need, to have to.

w: מִצִּדּוֹ שֶׁל|of|~lit. from the side of
s.line: “Thank you,” replied the girl; “that is very kind of Oz.”
s.note: נֶחְמָד מִצִּדְּךָ = "nice of you", literally "nice from your side". It is the standard polite phrase: זֶה מַמָּשׁ נֶחְמָד מִצִּדֵּךְ (to a woman).

s.line: The soldier now blew upon a green whistle,
s.note: שָׁרַק = to whistle, and מַשְׁרוֹקִית is the whistle itself. A football referee "whistles" a foul: הַשּׁוֹפֵט שָׁרַק.

s.line: and at once a young girl, dressed in a pretty green silk gown, entered the room.
s.note: The verb comes before its subject here (<t>נִכְנְסָה … נַעֲרָה</t>), common in Hebrew when someone new appears. In <t>שִׂמְלַת מֶשִׁי יְרֻקָּה</t> the adjective agrees with <t>שִׂמְלָה</t>, the first noun of the construct, not with <t>מֶשִׁי</t>.

w: הָיָה לָהּ|she had|~lit. there was to her
s.line: She had lovely green hair and green eyes,
and she bowed low before Dorothy as she said, “Follow me and I will show you your room.”
s.note: קָדָה קִידָה, verb + noun from the same root, as you know. הֶרְאָה (hif'il of רָאָה) = to show, "to make see"; אַרְאֶה לָךְ = I'll show you (to a woman).

s.line: So Dorothy said good-bye to all her friends except Toto,
s.note: נִפְרַד מִ… (nif'al, active meaning) = to say goodbye to, to part from; הִפְרִיד (hif'il) = to separate. A couple that splits up נִפְרְדוּ.

w: עַל הַיָּדַיִם|in her arms|~lit. on the hands
s.line: and taking the dog in her arms followed the green girl through seven passages and up three flights of stairs until they came to a room at the front of the Palace.
s.note: לָקַח עַל הַיָּדַיִם = to pick up and carry in one's arms, said of babies and pets. Number gender: מִסְדְּרוֹן is masculine (שִׁבְעָה), קוֹמָה feminine (שָׁלוֹשׁ).

s.line: It was the sweetest little room in the world,
s.note: הֲכִי + adjective is the everyday superlative: הֲכִי חָמוּד = the cutest. חָמוּד (cute, sweet) is what Israelis say about babies, puppies and small rooms alike.

s.line: with a soft comfortable bed that had sheets of green silk and a green velvet counterpane.
There was a tiny fountain in the middle of the room, that shot a spray of green perfume into the air,
s.note: הִתִּיז (hif'il) = to spray, splash; the nun of the root נ־ת־ז drops and leaves a dagesh in the ת. סִילוֹן = a jet of liquid; a jet plane is מְטוֹס סִילוֹן.

s.line: to fall back into a beautifully carved green marble basin.
s.note: מְגֻלָּף (carved) is pu'al, the passive of pi'el גִּלֵּף (to carve, engrave). Pu'al participles are the usual way to say "made by hand in some way": מְצֻיָּר painted, מְקֻשָּׁט decorated.

s.line: Beautiful green flowers stood in the windows, and there was a shelf with a row of little green books.
When Dorothy had time to open these books she found them full of queer green pictures that made her laugh, they were so funny.
s.note: כָּל כָּךְ … שֶׁ… = "so … that …". מַצְחִיק (funny) is a hif'il participle, "making laugh", the causative of צָחַק (to laugh). מָלֵא takes בְּ or nothing: מָלֵא בִּתְמוּנוֹת, מְלֵא אֲנָשִׁים.

s.line: In a wardrobe were many green dresses, made of silk and satin and velvet;
and all of them fitted Dorothy exactly.
s.note: בַּמִּדָּה שֶׁלִּי = "my size", what you ask for in a clothes shop: יֵשׁ לָכֶם אֶת זֶה בַּמִּדָּה שֶׁלִּי? כֻּלָּן is the feminine plural "all of them", because שְׂמָלוֹת are feminine.

w: כְּמוֹ בַּבַּיִת|at home|~lit. like at home
s.line: “Make yourself perfectly at home,” said the green girl, “and if you wish for anything ring the bell.
s.note: תַּרְגִּישִׁי כְּמוֹ בַּבַּיִת = make yourself at home, said to every guest. צִלְצֵל = to ring; it is also the everyday "to phone": אֲנִי אֲצַלְצֵל אֵלֶיךָ מָחָר. Note the preposition: צִלְצֵל בַּפַּעֲמוֹן.

s.line: Oz will send for you tomorrow morning.”
She left Dorothy alone and went back to the others.
These she also led to rooms, and each one of them found himself lodged in a very pleasant part of the Palace.
s.note: מְשֻׁכָּן (housed, lodged) is a pu'al participle of שִׁכֵּן (to house). The root שׁ־כ־ן gives שָׁכֵן (neighbour), שְׁכוּנָה (neighbourhood) and שִׁכּוּן (a housing block). Putting the object first (גַּם אוֹתָם הִיא הוֹבִילָה) stresses it, like English "these she also led".

w: הָלַךְ לְאִבּוּד|was wasted|~lit. went to loss
s.line: Of course this politeness was wasted on the Scarecrow;
s.note: הָלַךְ לְאִבּוּד = got lost, went to waste: הַמִּכְתָּב הָלַךְ לְאִבּוּד (the letter got lost). For money or effort you can also say הִתְבַּזְבֵּז (was wasted).

s.line: for when he found himself alone in his room he stood stupidly in one spot, just within the doorway, to wait till morning.
s.note: חִכָּה לְ… = to wait for: אֲנִי מְחַכֶּה לְךָ. The preposition is לְ, not a separate word for "for".

s.line: It would not rest him to lie down, and he could not close his eyes;
s.note: עָצַם עֵינַיִם = to close one's eyes; for a door or a book you use סָגַר. לֹא עָצַמְתִּי עַיִן כָּל הַלַּיְלָה = I didn't sleep a wink.

s.line: so he remained all night staring at a little spider which was weaving its web in a corner of the room,
s.note: בָּהָה בְּ… = to stare blankly at; בָּהָה בַּטֶּלֶוִיזְיָה. A spider's web is קוּרֵי עַכָּבִישׁ; טָוָה = to spin or weave, and טָוָה תָּכְנִית = to hatch a plan.

s.line: just as if it were not one of the most wonderful rooms in the world.
s.note: בְּיוֹתֵר after an adjective is the written superlative (הַנִּפְלָאִים בְּיוֹתֵר); in speech הֲכִי נִפְלָאִים means the same.

s.line: The Tin Woodman lay down on his bed from force of habit, for he remembered when he was made of flesh;
s.note: מִכֹּחַ הַהֶרְגֵּל = out of habit, exactly as in English. הִתְרַגֵּל לְ… = to get used to.

s.line: but not being able to sleep, he passed the night moving his joints up and down to make sure they kept in good working order.
s.note: בִּלָּה (pi'el) = to spend time; on its own it means to have a good time: בִּלִּינוּ יָפֶה (we had fun), and בִּלּוּי is an outing. לְוַדֵּא = to make sure, from the same root as וַדַּאי (certainly).

s.line: The Lion would have preferred a bed of dried leaves in the forest, and did not like being shut up in a room;
s.note: הָיָה מַעֲדִיף = "would have preferred": הָיָה + participle also makes the conditional ("would"), besides the past habit you met in chapter 1. הֶעֱדִיף = to prefer: אֲנִי מַעֲדִיף קָפֶה.

w: הָיָה לוֹ|he had|~lit. there was to him
s.line: but he had too much sense to let this worry him,
s.note: נָתַן לְ… + infinitive = to let, allow: תֵּן לִי לַחְשֹׁב (let me think). הִטְרִיד = to bother, trouble; מַה מַּטְרִיד אוֹתְךָ? = what's bothering you?

s.line: so he sprang upon the bed and rolled himself up like a cat and purred himself asleep in a minute.
s.note: הִתְכַּרְבֵּל = to curl up, snuggle (into a blanket: הִתְכַּרְבֵּל בִּשְׂמִיכָה). נִרְדַּם (nif'al, active meaning) = fell asleep; הִרְדִּים (hif'il) = to put to sleep, also used of anaesthesia.

s.line: The next morning, after breakfast, the green maiden came to fetch Dorothy,
and she dressed her in one of the prettiest gowns, made of green brocaded satin.
s.note: One root, three binyanim: לָבַשׁ (pa'al) = to put on, wear; הִלְבִּישׁ (hif'il) = to dress someone else; הִתְלַבֵּשׁ (hitpa'el) = to get dressed. רָקוּם = embroidered, from רָקַם; רָקַם תָּכְנִית = to work out a plan.

s.line: Dorothy put on a green silk apron and tied a green ribbon around Toto’s neck,
s.note: סֶרֶט = ribbon, and also a film: הָלַכְנוּ לִרְאוֹת סֶרֶט. סְבִיב is the preposition "around"; סָבִיב is the adverb "all around".

w: יָצְאוּ לַדֶּרֶךְ|set off|~lit. went out to the road
s.line: and they started for the Throne Room of the Great Oz.

w: בִּגְדֵי פְּאֵר|rich costumes|~lit. clothes of splendour
s.line: First they came to a great hall in which were many ladies and gentlemen of the court, all dressed in rich costumes.
s.note: גְּבִירוֹתַי וְרַבּוֹתַי is how a speaker opens a speech: "ladies and gentlemen". חָצֵר is a royal court here, but in daily life it is a yard: הַיְּלָדִים מְשַׂחֲקִים בֶּחָצֵר.

s.line: These people had nothing to do but talk to each other,
s.note: לֹא הָיָה לָהֶם מָה לַעֲשׂוֹת = they had nothing to do. אֵין לִי מָה לְהַגִּיד = I have nothing to say. The pattern is אֵין / לֹא הָיָה + מָה + infinitive.

w: מִחוּץ לַחֲדַר הַכֵּס|outside the Throne Room
s.line: but they always came to wait outside the Throne Room every morning, although they were never permitted to see Oz.
s.note: הֻרְשָׁה (was permitted) is hof'al, the passive of hif'il הִרְשָׁה (to allow). The hof'al participle מֻרְשֶׁה = authorized, and רִשְׁיוֹן (licence) is from the same root.

s.line: As Dorothy entered they looked at her curiously, and one of them whispered:
“Are you really going to look upon the face of Oz the Terrible?”
s.note: הוֹלֵךְ לְ… + infinitive = "going to", the spoken near future, just like English. פָּנִים (face) is always plural in form; פְּנֵי is its construct.

s.line: “Of course,” answered the girl, “if he will see me.”
s.note: After <t>אִם</t> Hebrew uses the future for a future condition: <t>אִם יֵרֵד גֶּשֶׁם, נִשָּׁאֵר בַּבַּיִת</t>. <t>הִסְכִּים</t> = to agree; <t>הֶסְכֵּם</t> = an agreement, a word you will see in the news.

s.line: “Oh, he will see you,” said the soldier who had taken her message to the Wizard, “although he does not like to have people ask to see him.
Indeed, at first he was angry and said I should send you back where you came from.
s.note: אָמַר שֶׁ… + future = "said I should": an order in reported speech. כָּעַס = to be angry, a verb in Hebrew (אַל תִּכְעַס = don't be angry); כָּעַס עַל = angry at.

s.line: Then he asked me what you looked like,
s.note: "What you looked like" is אֵיךְ אַתְּ נִרְאֵית, "how you look", and in the present tense: a reported question keeps the tense of the original question.

s.line: and when I mentioned your silver shoes he was very much interested.
s.note: הִזְכִּיר (hif'il) = to mention or to remind; זָכַר (pa'al) = to remember. הִתְעַנְיֵן בְּ… = to be interested in; מְעַנְיֵן = interesting.

s.line: At last I told him about the mark upon your forehead,
and he decided he would admit you to his presence.”
Just then a bell rang,
and the green girl said to Dorothy, “That is the signal.
s.note: אוֹת = a sign or signal, and also a letter of the alphabet (plural אוֹתִיּוֹת). Don't confuse it with אוֹתוֹ / אוֹתָךְ, the object pronouns.

s.line: You must go into the Throne Room alone.”
She opened a little door and Dorothy walked boldly through and found herself in a wonderful place.
It was a big, round room with a high arched roof,
s.note: מְקֻמָּר (arched, vaulted) is a pu'al participle; the arch itself is קֶשֶׁת or קִמְרוֹן. קֶשֶׁת is also a rainbow and a bow for arrows.

s.line: and the walls and ceiling and floor were covered with large emeralds set closely together.
s.note: מְכֻסֶּה (covered) is pu'al, the passive of pi'el כִּסָּה (to cover); מִכְסֶה = a lid. Mixed masculine and feminine nouns (קִירוֹת, תִּקְרָה, רִצְפָּה) take the masculine plural: מְכֻסִּים.

s.line: In the center of the roof was a great light, as bright as the sun, which made the emeralds sparkle in a wonderful manner.
s.note: גָּרַם לְ… + infinitive = to make something happen: הַסֶּרֶט גָּרַם לִי לִבְכּוֹת (the film made me cry). בְּאֹפֶן + adjective is a written way to make an adverb: בְּאֹפֶן נִפְלָא = wonderfully.

s.line: But what interested Dorothy most was the big throne of green marble that stood in the middle of the room.
s.note: עִנְיֵן (pi'el) = to interest someone: זֶה לֹא מְעַנְיֵן אוֹתִי = I don't care about that. Compare הִתְעַנְיֵן בְּ (hitpa'el) from the soldier's story: the thing interests (מְעַנְיֵן), the person is interested (מִתְעַנְיֵן).

s.line: It was shaped like a chair and sparkled with gems, as did everything else.
s.note: אֲבָנִים טוֹבוֹת ("good stones") = precious stones, gems. אֶבֶן is feminine, so טוֹבוֹת. בְּצוּרַת = "in the shape of": עוּגָה בְּצוּרַת לֵב.

s.line: In the center of the chair was an enormous Head, without a body to support it or any arms or legs whatever.
s.note: יָד covers hand and arm, and רֶגֶל foot and leg; both are feminine and come in the dual (יָדַיִם, רַגְלַיִם). הֶחְזִיק (hif'il) = to hold, hold up.

w: הָיוּ לוֹ|it had|~lit. there were to it
s.line: There was no hair upon this head, but it had eyes and a nose and mouth,
s.note: אַף = nose, and it is spelled exactly like אַף "even, not even" in אַף אֶחָד. Another meaning is anger: אַף in אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם (patient, slow to anger).

s.line: and was much bigger than the head of the biggest giant.
As Dorothy gazed upon this in wonder and fear, the eyes turned slowly and looked at her sharply and steadily.
s.note: הִבִּיט בְּ… takes בְּ, while הִסְתַּכֵּל takes עַל: הִבִּיטָה בּוֹ = הִסְתַּכְּלָה עָלָיו. הִבִּיט בְּמַבָּט is verb + noun from one root, like קָדָה קִידָה.

s.line: Then the mouth moved, and Dorothy heard a voice say:
“I am Oz, the Great and Terrible.
Who are you, and why do you seek me?”
s.note: הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא echoes the prayer book, where God is הָאֵל הַגָּדוֹל הַגִּבּוֹר וְהַנּוֹרָא. נוֹרָא literally means "awesome, fearsome"; in modern speech it mostly means "terrible": הָיָה נוֹרָא = it was awful.

s.line: It was not such an awful voice as she had expected to come from the big Head;
s.note: צִפָּה (pi'el) = to expect, צִפִּיָּה = expectation. In pa'al, צָפָה (same letters without vowels) = to watch, or to float. צָפִיתָ בַּסֶּרֶט? = did you watch the film?

s.line: so she took courage and answered:
s.note: אָזַר אֹמֶץ = to pluck up courage, still the standard phrase: אָזַרְתִּי אֹמֶץ וְשָׁאַלְתִּי. The verb אָזַר (to gird) is hardly used outside this phrase.

s.line: “I am Dorothy, the Small and Meek.
s.note: עֲנָוָה here is the feminine of עָנָו (humble, meek). The same spelling is also the noun "humility": בְּכָל הָעֲנָוָה = in all humility. Dorothy's title copies Oz's pattern הַ… וְהַ….

s.line: I have come to you for help.”
The eyes looked at her thoughtfully for a full minute.
s.note: הִרְהוּר = musing, reflection; the verb is הִרְהֵר (to ponder). הִרְהוּרִים is a common title for opinion columns. דַּקָּה שְׁלֵמָה = a whole minute, with no word for "for".

s.line: Then said the voice:
“Where did you get the silver shoes?”
s.note: הִשִּׂיג = to obtain, get hold of: אֵיךְ הִשַּׂגְתָּ כַּרְטִיסִים? (how did you get tickets?). Its noun הֶשֵּׂג = an achievement.

w: מֵהַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמִּזְרָח|from the Wicked Witch of the East
s.line: “I got them from the Wicked Witch of the East, when my house fell on her and killed her,” she replied.
s.note: אוֹתָן is "them" for feminine plurals, because נַעֲלַיִם are feminine; for the masculine it would be אוֹתָם.

s.line: “Where did you get the mark upon your forehead?” continued the voice.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הַטּוֹבָה מֵהַצָּפוֹן|the Good Witch of the North
s.line: “That is where the Good Witch of the North kissed me when she bade me good-bye and sent me to you,” said the girl.
s.note: נִשְּׁקָה looks like a nif'al, but it is the pi'el נִשֵּׁק (to kiss), whose first root letter is נ. Watch the dagesh in the שּׁ. "Kiss someone" is נִשֵּׁק לְ…; נְשִׁיקָה = a kiss.

s.line: Again the eyes looked at her sharply, and they saw she was telling the truth.
s.note: הֵן: עֵינַיִם are feminine, so "they" is הֵן. As in chapter 1, the reported verb stays in the present (אוֹמֶרֶת) where English says "was telling".

s.line: Then Oz asked, “What do you wish me to do?”
s.note: "Want someone to do" is רוֹצֶה שֶׁ… + future: אֲנִי רוֹצָה שֶׁתָּבוֹא = I want you to come. Hebrew cannot say "want me to do" with an infinitive.

s.line: “Send me back to Kansas, where my Aunt Em and Uncle Henry are,” she answered earnestly.
s.note: תַּחֲזִיר: a future verb as a request, softer than the imperative הַחְזֵר. הֶחְזִיר (hif'il) = to return something or someone; חָזַר (pa'al) = to come back. נִמְצָא (nif'al, "is found") is the normal "to be located": אֵיפֹה נִמְצָא הַבַּנְק?

s.line: “I don’t like your country, although it is so beautiful.
And I am sure Aunt Em will be dreadfully worried over my being away so long.”
s.note: מֻדְאָג (worried) is a hof'al participle, "made to worry", from hif'il הִדְאִיג (to worry someone): זֶה מַדְאִיג אוֹתִי. נֶעְדַּר = to be absent; in the news נֶעְדָּר is a missing person. נוֹרָא before or after an adjective = "terribly, really": נוֹרָא יָפֶה.

s.line: The eyes winked three times,
s.note: קָרַץ = to wink, and קָרַץ לְ… = to appeal to: הָרַעְיוֹן הַזֶּה לֹא קוֹרֵץ לִי = that idea doesn't appeal to me. פַּעַם is feminine, so it is שָׁלוֹשׁ פְּעָמִים.

s.line: and then they turned up to the ceiling and down to the floor and rolled around so queerly that they seemed to see every part of the room.
s.note: הִתְגַּלְגֵּל = to roll (by itself); גִּלְגֵּל (pi'el) = to roll something, and גַּלְגַּל is a wheel. פָּנָה = to turn (פְּנֵה יָמִינָה = turn right), and פָּנָה אֶל = to address someone.

s.line: And at last they looked at Dorothy again.
“Why should I do this for you?” asked Oz.
s.note: לָמָּה שֶׁ… + future = "why should …?", a common rhetorical question: לָמָּה שֶׁאַסְכִּים? = why should I agree? בִּשְׁבִילֵךְ is "for you" to a woman; to a man, בִּשְׁבִילְךָ.

s.line: “Because you are strong and I am weak;
because you are a Great Wizard and I am only a little girl.”
s.note: Hebrew needs no "am / are" in the present: <t>אַתָּה חָזָק</t> = you are strong. Note the gender pairs: <t>חָזָק</t> / <t>חֲזָקָה</t>, <t>חַלָּשׁ</t> / <t>חַלָּשָׁה</t>.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמִּזְרָח|the Wicked Witch of the East
s.line: “But you were strong enough to kill the Wicked Witch of the East,” said Oz.
s.note: מַסְפִּיק comes after the adjective, as in English: חֲזָקָה מַסְפִּיק = strong enough. As a verb it means "it is enough": מַסְפִּיק! = that's enough!

s.line: “That just happened,” returned Dorothy simply;
s.note: פָּשׁוּט = simple, and as an adverb "just, simply": פָּשׁוּט תִּשְׁאַל = just ask. בְּפַשְׁטוּת = in a simple, plain way.

s.line: “I could not help it.”
s.note: מָנַע = to prevent; מְנִיעָה = prevention, and אֵין מְנִיעָה = "there's no objection", a phrase heard in offices.

s.line: “Well,” said the Head, “I will give you my answer.

w: אֵין לָךְ|you have no|~lit. there is not to you
s.line: You have no right to expect me to send you back to Kansas unless you do something for me in return.
s.note: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן = unless, followed by the future here. בִּתְמוּרָה = in return, in exchange; תְּמוּרָה is also the word for a company's turnover in business news.

s.line: In this country everyone must pay for everything he gets.
s.note: The same idea in a modern saying: אֵין אֲרוּחוֹת חִנָּם = there's no such thing as a free lunch. חַיָּב = must, have to; it also means "owe": אַתָּה חַיָּב לִי כֶּסֶף.

s.line: If you wish me to use my magic power to send you home again you must do something for me first.
s.note: הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּ… = to use, always with בְּ: אֲנִי מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בַּמַּחְשֵׁב. In hitpa'el the ת and a first root letter שׁ swap places: הִתְשַׁמֵּשׁ → הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ. הַבַּיְתָה = homeward; the unstressed ending ה means "to", as in יָמִינָה.

s.line: Help me and I will help you.”
s.note: עָזַר לְ… takes לְ, not אֶת: אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲזֹר לְךָ? = can I help you?, which is what a shop assistant says.

s.line: “What must I do?” asked the girl.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: “Kill the Wicked Witch of the West,” answered Oz.
s.note: הִרְגִי is the short imperative to a woman. Here, for a hard command, Oz uses it rather than the softer future form (תַּהַרְגִי).

s.line: “But I cannot!” exclaimed Dorothy, greatly surprised.
s.note: מֻפְתָּע (surprised) is a hof'al participle, the passive of hif'il הִפְתִּיעַ (to surprise); הַפְתָּעָה = a surprise, as in מְסִבַּת הַפְתָּעָה. קָרָא = to call out, besides "to read".

w: שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶן|which have|~lit. that there is in them
s.line: “You killed the Witch of the East and you wear the silver shoes, which bear a powerful charm.
s.note: נָעַל = to put on or wear shoes (נַעַל = shoe), so shoes are "shod", never "worn" with לָבַשׁ. The same verb means "to lock": נָעַלְתִּי אֶת הַדֶּלֶת.

s.line: There is now but one Wicked Witch left in all this land,
s.note: נִשְׁאַר (nif'al, active meaning) = to remain, be left, and it agrees with what is left: נִשְׁאֲרָה for a witch, נִשְׁאַר לִי שֶׁקֶל (I have a shekel left).

s.line: and when you can tell me she is dead I will send you back to Kansas—but not before.”
s.note: After כְּשֶׁ about the future, Hebrew uses the future (כְּשֶׁתּוּכְלִי), where English uses the present "when you can". לִפְנֵי כֵן = before that, beforehand.

s.line: The little girl began to weep, she was so much disappointed;
s.note: מְאֻכְזֶבֶת (disappointed) has the shape of a pu'al participle, like מְאֻשָּׁר, from a four-letter root א־כ־ז־ב. The active form is אִכְזֵב = to let someone down (הוּא אִכְזֵב אוֹתִי), and הִתְאַכְזֵב = to be disappointed. אַכְזָבָה = a disappointment.

s.line: and the eyes winked again and looked upon her anxiously, as if the Great Oz felt that she could help him if she would.
s.note: הִבִּיט בְּ־ = to look at: the verb takes בְּ, so "at her" is בָּהּ. אִם רַק = "if only, if she just …", followed by the future תִּרְצֶה.

w: מֵרְצוֹנִי|of my own will|~lit. from my will
s.line: “I never killed anything, willingly,” she sobbed.
s.note: מֵרְצוֹנִי = "of my own free will", from רָצוֹן (will, wish), the same root as רָצָה (wanted). You will hear מֵרְצוֹן in news reports: הִתְפַּטֵּר מֵרְצוֹנוֹ = resigned of his own accord.

s.line: “Even if I wanted to, how could I kill the Wicked Witch?
s.note: הָיִיתִי רוֹצָה, הָיִיתִי יְכוֹלָה: הָיָה + participle is also the everyday conditional, "would / could": הָיִיתִי בָּא, אֲבָל אֵין לִי זְמַן = I would come, but I have no time.

s.line: If you, who are Great and Terrible, cannot kill her yourself, how do you expect me to do it?”
s.note: צִפָּה (pi'el) = to expect: מְצַפֶּה שֶׁ… + future, or מְצַפֶּה לְ… + noun (אֲנִי מְצַפֶּה לִתְשׁוּבָה = I'm waiting for an answer). בְּעַצְמְךָ = yourself, by yourself.

s.line: “I do not know,” said the Head;
“but that is my answer, and until the Wicked Witch dies you will not see your uncle and aunt again.
s.note: עַד שֶׁ… לֹא: after עַד שֶׁ ("until"), Hebrew often adds a לֹא that means nothing: עַד שֶׁהַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה לֹא תָּמוּת = until the Witch dies. It is very common in speech: לֹא נֵצֵא עַד שֶׁהַגֶּשֶׁם לֹא יַפְסִיק = we won't go out until the rain stops.

s.line: Remember that the Witch is Wicked—tremendously Wicked—and ought to be killed.
s.note: בְּצוּרָה נוֹרָאִית ("in a terrible way") is how modern Hebrew turns an adjective into an adverb: בְּצוּרָה טוֹבָה = well. צָרִיךְ לַהֲרֹג אוֹתָהּ with no subject = "she must be killed", the same impersonal trick as הָיָה צָרִיךְ in chapter 1.

s.line: Now go, and do not ask to see me again until you have done your task.”
s.note: אַל + future = "don't …", the negative command: אַל תְּבַקְשִׁי (don't ask, to a woman), אַל תִּדְאַג (don't worry, to a man). You never use לֹא with the imperative itself. מְשִׂימָה = task, mission.

s.line: Sorrowfully Dorothy left the Throne Room and went back where the Lion and the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman were waiting to hear what Oz had said to her.
s.note: יָצָא מִ־ = to leave (go out of) a place. שֶׁבּוֹ = "in which, where" (literally "that in it"); with a feminine noun it is שֶׁבָּהּ: הָעִיר שֶׁבָּהּ גָּדַלְתִּי = the town where I grew up. חִכָּה לְ־ = to wait for.

w: אֵין לִי|I have no|~lit. there isn't to me
s.line: “There is no hope for me,” she said sadly,

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: “for Oz will not send me home until I have killed the Wicked Witch of the West;
s.note: הַבַּיְתָה = "(to) home". The ending ָה marks direction "to": צָפוֹנָה northward, יָמִינָה to the right. After עַד שֶׁ Hebrew uses the future (אֶהֱרֹג) where English says "have killed".

s.line: and that I can never do.”
s.note: אוּכַל is the future of יָכוֹל (can): אוּכַל, תּוּכַל, יוּכַל, נוּכַל. It is irregular, so learn it as a set. אֶת זֶה comes first for emphasis: "that, I can never do".

s.line: Her friends were sorry, but could do nothing to help her;
s.note: הִצְטַעֵר (hitpa'el) = to be sorry, to regret; the hitpa'el ת swaps places with the צ of the root (הִתְצַעֵר → הִצְטַעֵר). The everyday "I'm sorry" is אֲנִי מִצְטַעֵר or צַר לִי.

s.line: so Dorothy went to her own room and lay down on the bed and cried herself to sleep.
s.note: Two nif'al verbs with active meaning: נִשְׁכַּב = to lie down (שָׁכַב = to be lying) and נִרְדַּם = to fall asleep. יָשַׁן is "to sleep", נִרְדַּם is the moment of dropping off.

s.line: The next morning the soldier with the green whiskers came to the Scarecrow and said:
s.note: לְמָחֳרָת = "on the next day" (in a story), while מָחָר = tomorrow (from now). Note the order here: time first, then verb, then subject (בָּא הַחַיָּל). This is common in Hebrew narrative.

w: שָׁלַח לִקְרֹא לְךָ|sent for you|~lit. sent to call to you
s.line: “Come with me, for Oz has sent for you.”
s.note: שָׁלַח לִקְרֹא לְ־ = "sent for (someone)". קָרָא לְ־ = to call someone over: תִּקְרָא לוֹ = call him (to come).

s.line: So the Scarecrow followed him and was admitted into the great Throne Room,
s.note: הָלַךְ אַחֲרֵי = to follow (literally "go after"). הִכְנִיסוּ אוֹתוֹ = "they let him in" with no subject, Hebrew's usual way to say "he was admitted". הִכְנִיס (hif'il) = to bring in; נִכְנַס (nif'al) = to go in.

s.line: where he saw, sitting in the emerald throne, a most lovely Lady.
s.note: מַקְסִים = charming, lovely, a hif'il participle of ק־ס־ם (magic), the same root as קוֹסֵם (wizard): literally "enchanting". גְּבֶרֶת = lady; גְּבִירוֹתַי וְרַבּוֹתַי = ladies and gentlemen.

s.line: She was dressed in green silk gauze and wore upon her flowing green locks a crown of jewels.
s.note: חָבַשׁ is the verb for wearing something on the head (a hat, a crown, a helmet); clothes take לָבַשׁ, hence לְבוּשָׁה "dressed". גּוֹלֵשׁ = flowing, sliding down; today גּוֹלֵשׁ is also a surfer or a skier, and לִגְלֹשׁ בָּאִינְטֶרְנֶט = to surf the web.

s.line: Growing from her shoulders were wings, gorgeous in color and so light that they fluttered if the slightest breath of air reached them.
s.note: כְּנָפַיִם is a dual and feminine, so "they" is הֵן and the adjective is קַלּוֹת. מַשַּׁב רוּחַ = a gust or breath of wind. נָגַע בְּ־ = to touch (with בְּ). הַקַּל בְּיוֹתֵר = the lightest: בְּיוֹתֵר after an adjective makes the superlative.

s.line: When the Scarecrow had bowed, as prettily as his straw stuffing would let him, before this beautiful creature,
s.note: כְּכָל שֶׁ… = "as much as, as far as": כְּכָל שֶׁאֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ = as far as I know. הִרְשָׁה לְ־ = to allow someone; the noun is רְשׁוּת (permission) and the adjective מֻרְשֶׁה (allowed, authorized). קָד (bowed): as in קָד קִידָה.

s.line: she looked upon him sweetly, and said:

w: אוֹז הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא|Oz the Great and Terrible
s.line: “I am Oz, the Great and Terrible.
s.note: The Lady keeps the title <t>אוֹז הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא</t> in the masculine, because it is a fixed title. Elsewhere in this scene, when Oz appears as the Lady, the verbs are feminine (as Baum says "she").

s.line: Who are you, and why do you seek me?”
Now the Scarecrow, who had expected to see the great Head Dorothy had told him of, was much astonished;
s.note: שֶׁדּוֹרוֹתִי סִפְּרָה לוֹ עָלָיו = "that Dorothy told him about (it)". In a Hebrew relative clause the preposition stays behind with a pronoun (עָלָיו) pointing back to הָרֹאשׁ. English drops it ("the Head Dorothy had told him of"), but Hebrew needs it. נִדְהַם = to be amazed; מַדְהִים = amazing.

s.line: but he answered her bravely.
“I am only a Scarecrow, stuffed with straw.
s.note: מְמֻלָּא (stuffed, filled) is a pu'al participle of מִלֵּא (pi'el, to fill). Pi'el and pu'al are an active/passive pair: מִלֵּא filled → מֻלָּא was filled. In the kitchen, פִּלְפֵּל מְמֻלָּא = stuffed pepper.

w: אֵין לִי|I have no|~lit. there isn't to me
s.line: Therefore I have no brains, and I come to you praying that you will put brains in my head instead of straw,
s.note: הִתְחַנֵּן (hitpa'el) = to beg, plead, from the root of חֵן (grace, favor): you ask for someone's favor. בִּמְקוֹם = "instead of", literally "in the place of": תֵּה בִּמְקוֹם קָפֶה = tea instead of coffee.

s.line: so that I may become as much a man as any other in your dominions.”
s.note: כְּדֵי שֶׁ + future = "so that": דַּבֵּר לְאַט כְּדֵי שֶׁאָבִין = speak slowly so that I understand. With the same subject you use כְּדֵי + infinitive instead: בָּאתִי כְּדֵי לַעֲזֹר.

s.line: “Why should I do this for you?” asked the Lady.
s.note: לָמָּה שֶׁ… + future = "why should …?", a very common spoken pattern: לָמָּה שֶׁאֶשְׁלַם יוֹתֵר? = why should I pay more?

w: וְאַף אֶחָד|and no one|~with לֹא: nobody
s.line: “Because you are wise and powerful, and no one else can help me,” answered the Scarecrow.

w: עוֹשָׂה טוֹבוֹת|do favors|~idiom: עָשָׂה טוֹבָה = did a favor
s.line: “I never grant favors without some return,” said Oz;
s.note: עָשָׂה טוֹבָה = to do a favor: תַּעֲשֶׂה לִי טוֹבָה = do me a favor (also said sarcastically, "give me a break"). בִּתְמוּרָה = in return, in exchange. The verb is אָמְרָה (feminine) because Oz appears as a lady.

s.line: “but this much I will promise.
s.note: הִבְטִיחַ (hif'il) = to promise; הַבְטָחָה = a promise. From the same root: בָּטוּחַ = sure, safe, and בִּטָּחוֹן = security.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: If you will kill for me the Wicked Witch of the West, I will bestow upon you a great many brains, and such good brains that you will be the wisest man in all the Land of Oz.”
s.note: הֶעֱנִיק (hif'il) = to grant, award, a higher-register word for "give": הֶעֱנִיקוּ לוֹ פְּרָס = he was awarded a prize. מַעֲנָק = a grant (of money). In everyday speech אֶתֵּן לְךָ would do.

s.line: “I thought you asked Dorothy to kill the Witch,” said the Scarecrow, in surprise.
s.note: בִּקֵּשׁ מִ־ = to ask (something) of someone: you ask "from" a person, בִּקַּשְׁתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ עֶזְרָה = I asked him for help. To ask a question is שָׁאַל.

s.line: “So I did.
I don’t care who kills her.
s.note: לֹא אִכְפַּת לִי = I don't care. The person goes after לְ: אִכְפַּת לוֹ = he cares. אִכְפַּת לְךָ…? = "do you mind …?": אִכְפַּת לְךָ לִסְגֹּר אֶת הַחַלּוֹן?

s.line: But until she is dead I will not grant your wish.
s.note: מִלֵּא מִשְׁאָלָה = to grant a wish, literally "to fill a wish", from the same pi'el מִלֵּא (to fill) as מְמֻלָּא above. כָּל עוֹד = as long as; בַּחַיִּים = alive, among the living.

s.line: Now go, and do not seek me again until you have earned the brains you so greatly desire.”
s.note: הִרְוִיחַ (hif'il) = to earn, to make a profit: כַּמָּה אַתָּה מַרְוִיחַ? = how much do you earn? רֶוַח = profit. הִרְוַחְנוּ זְמַן = we gained time.

s.line: The Scarecrow went sorrowfully back to his friends and told them what Oz had said;
and Dorothy was surprised to find that the Great Wizard was not a Head, as she had seen him, but a lovely Lady.
s.note: הֻפְתְּעָה is hof'al, the passive of the hif'il הִפְתִּיעַ (to surprise): הוּא הִפְתִּיעַ אוֹתָהּ → הִיא הֻפְתְּעָה. The noun is הַפְתָּעָה. לֹא X אֶלָּא Y = "not X but (rather) Y". After a negative, use אֶלָּא rather than אֲבָל.

s.line: “All the same,” said the Scarecrow,
s.note: בְּכָל זֹאת = "even so, still, nevertheless", very common in speech: הָיָה קַר, וּבְכָל זֹאת יָצָאנוּ = it was cold, and still we went out.

s.line: “she needs a heart as much as the Tin Woodman.”
s.note: צָרִיךְ + noun = to need: אֲנִי צָרִיךְ עֶזְרָה. It agrees like an adjective: צָרִיךְ, צְרִיכָה, צְרִיכִים. לֹא פָּחוֹת מִ־ = "no less than", a common way to say "just as much as".

s.line: On the next morning the soldier with the green whiskers came to the Tin Woodman and said:

w: שָׁלַח לִקְרֹא לְךָ|sent for you|~lit. sent to call to you
s.line: “Oz has sent for you.
Follow me.”
So the Tin Woodman followed him and came to the great Throne Room.
He did not know whether he would find Oz a lovely Lady or a Head, but he hoped it would be the lovely Lady.
s.note: אִם means both "if" and "whether": אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ אִם הוּא בַּבַּיִת. קִוָּה (pi'el) = to hope, from the root of תִּקְוָה (hope). דְּמוּת = figure, form; also a character in a book or film.

s.line: “For,” he said to himself, “if it is the head, I am sure I shall not be given a heart,
s.note: לֹא יִתְּנוּ לִי = "they won't give me", with no subject, the everyday Hebrew for "I shall not be given". אָמַר לְעַצְמוֹ = said to himself; עַצְמוֹ = himself.

s.line: since a head has no heart of its own and therefore cannot feel for me.
s.note: הֲרֵי = "after all, as we know", used to give a reason both sides already accept: הֲרֵי אָמַרְתִּי לְךָ = but I told you. רִחֵם עַל = to pity, to feel for; רַחֲמִים = mercy. מִשֶּׁלּוֹ = of its own.

s.line: But if it is the lovely Lady I shall beg hard for a heart,
for all ladies are themselves said to be kindly hearted.”
s.note: טוֹב לֵב = kind-hearted, an adjective in a construct pair ("good of heart"); only the first word changes: טוֹבַת לֵב, טוֹבֵי לֵב, טוֹבוֹת לֵב. The noun is טוּב לֵב (kindness).

w: לָבַשׁ דְּמוּת|had taken the form|~idiom: lit. put on a figure
s.line: But when the Woodman entered the great Throne Room he saw neither the Head nor the Lady, for Oz had taken the shape of a most terrible Beast.
s.note: לֹא … וְלֹא … = "neither … nor …": לֹא קַר וְלֹא חַם = neither cold nor hot. לָבַשׁ דְּמוּת = "put on the form of", i.e. took the shape of. לָבַשׁ is normally to put on clothes.

s.line: It was nearly as big as an elephant, and the green throne seemed hardly strong enough to hold its weight.
s.note: חַיָּה (animal, beast) is feminine, so "it" is הִיא and "its weight" is הַמִּשְׁקָל שֶׁלָּהּ. בְּקֹשִׁי = barely, hardly (from קָשֶׁה, hard). הֶחֱזִיק (hif'il) = to hold; חָזָק = strong, same root.

s.line: The Beast had a head like that of a rhinoceros, only there were five eyes in its face.
s.note: רַק שֶׁ… = "only, except that …". קַרְנַף (rhinoceros) is built from קֶרֶן (horn) + אַף (nose). חָמֵשׁ עֵינַיִם: עַיִן is feminine, so it takes the number form without ה.

w: וְהָיוּ לָהּ|and it had|~lit. there were to it
s.line: There were five long arms growing out of its body, and it also had five long, slim legs.
Thick, woolly hair covered every part of it,
s.note: כִּסָּה (pi'el) = to cover; מְכֻסֶּה (pu'al participle) = covered; כִּסּוּי = a lid, a cover. אוֹתָהּ כֻּלָּהּ = "all of it": כֹּל + suffix follows the noun or pronoun, as in הָעִיר כֻּלָּהּ (the whole city).

w: אִי אֶפְשָׁר|it was impossible|~lit. there is no possibility
s.line: and a more dreadful-looking monster could not be imagined.
s.note: אִי אֶפְשָׁר = impossible, "one can't"; in the past, אִי אֶפְשָׁר הָיָה. דִּמְיֵן = to imagine, a pi'el built from four letters (from דִּמְיוֹן, imagination). מַפְחִיד = scary, the hif'il "making afraid", vs פּוֹחֵד = afraid.

w: הָיָה דּוֹפֵק|would have beaten|pa'al ptc · ד־פ־ק
s.line: It was fortunate the Tin Woodman had no heart at that moment, for it would have beat loud and fast from terror.
s.note: מַזָּל שֶׁ… = "it's lucky that …", heard every day: מַזָּל שֶׁבָּאתָ! הָיָה דּוֹפֵק is the conditional ("would have beaten"). מֵרֹב + noun = "from so much …": מֵרֹב עֲיֵפוּת = from sheer tiredness.

s.line: But being only tin, the Woodman was not at all afraid, although he was much disappointed.
s.note: עָשׂוּי מִ־ = made of (a pa'ul participle of עָשָׂה): עָשׂוּי מֵעֵץ = made of wood. אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ = although; in speech לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ is just as common. הִתְאַכְזֵב goes with מְאֻכְזָב from earlier in this chapter.

w: אוֹז הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא|Oz the Great and Terrible
s.line: “I am Oz, the Great and Terrible,” spoke the Beast, in a voice that was one great roar.
s.note: שְׁאָגָה = a roar; the verb is שָׁאַג (to roar). Lions שׁוֹאֲגִים; in the news, a crowd or a jet engine can שָׁאַג too.

s.line: “Who are you, and why do you seek me?”

w: חוֹטֵב עֵצִים|a woodman|~lit. a cutter of trees
s.line: “I am a Woodman, and made of tin.

w: אֵין לִי|I have no|~lit. there isn't to me
s.line: Therefore I have no heart, and cannot love.
I pray you to give me a heart that I may be as other men are.”
s.note: בְּנֵי אָדָם = people, human beings (literally "sons of man"); one person is בֶּן אָדָם, and תִּהְיֶה בֶּן אָדָם! = be a decent person! שְׁאָר = the rest (of).

w: דָּרְשָׁה לָדַעַת|demanded|~idiom: lit. demanded to know
s.line: “Why should I do this?” demanded the Beast.
s.note: דָּרַשׁ לָדַעַת = "demanded to know", the usual way to render "demanded" with a question. דָּרַשׁ alone = to demand, require: הָעֲבוֹדָה דּוֹרֶשֶׁת נִסָּיוֹן = the job requires experience.

s.line: “Because I ask it, and you alone can grant my request,” answered the Woodman.
Oz gave a low growl at this, but said, gruffly:
s.note: נָהַם נְהִימָה = growled a growl, the verb + noun from the same root (as in קָד קִידָה). לְשֵׁמַע = "on hearing", a literary but still current phrase: לְשֵׁמַע הַחֲדָשׁוֹת = on hearing the news.

s.line: “If you indeed desire a heart, you must earn it.”
“How?” asked the Woodman.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: “Help Dorothy to kill the Wicked Witch of the West,” replied the Beast.
s.note: עָזַר לְ־ = to help someone: the person takes לְ, not אֶת: עֲזֹר לְדוֹרוֹתִי, תַּעַזְרִי לִי (help me).

s.line: “When the Witch is dead, come to me, and I will then give you the biggest and kindest and most loving heart in all the Land of Oz.”
s.note: הֲכִי + adjective is the everyday superlative: הֲכִי גָּדוֹל = biggest. הַגָּדוֹל בְּיוֹתֵר means the same and sounds a little more formal. After כְּשֶׁ about the future, Hebrew uses the future: כְּשֶׁהִיא תָּמוּת.

s.line: So the Tin Woodman was forced to return sorrowfully to his friends and tell them of the terrible Beast he had seen.
s.note: נֶאֱלַץ (nif'al) = was forced, had to; the active is pi'el אִלֵּץ (to force). אֲנִי נֶאֱלָץ and אֲנִי מֻכְרָח both mean "I am forced, I have no choice". In the news: הַטַּיָּס נֶאֱלַץ לִנְחֹת = the pilot was forced to land.

s.line: They all wondered greatly at the many forms the Great Wizard could take upon himself, and the Lion said:

w: בְּכָל הַכֹּחַ|with all my might|~lit. with all the strength
s.line: “If he is a Beast when I go to see him, I shall roar my loudest, and so frighten him that he will grant all I ask.
s.note: For a real future condition, Hebrew puts the future in both halves: אִם הוּא יִהְיֶה… אֶשְׁאַג, and also after כְּשֶׁ: כְּשֶׁאֵלֵךְ (when I go). English uses the present there. בְּכָל הַכֹּחַ = with all one's strength, "as hard as possible".

w: אֶעֱמִיד פָּנִים|I will pretend|~idiom: lit. set up a face
s.line: And if he is the lovely Lady, I shall pretend to spring upon her, and so compel her to do my bidding.
s.note: הֶעֱמִיד פָּנִים = to pretend (literally "to put up a face"): הוּא מַעֲמִיד פָּנִים שֶׁהוּא יָשֵׁן = he's pretending to be asleep. הִתְנַפֵּל עַל = to pounce on, attack, from נָפַל (fall): "to throw oneself on". הִכְרִיחַ = to force, compel.

w: נָתוּן לַחֲסָדַי|at my mercy|~idiom: lit. given to my kindnesses
s.line: And if he is the great Head, he will be at my mercy;
s.note: נָתוּן לְחַסְדֵי… = "at the mercy of …", a set phrase still used in writing and the news: הַסִּירָה הָיְתָה נְתוּנָה לְחַסְדֵי הַגַּלִּים = the boat was at the mercy of the waves. נָתוּן is the pa'ul participle of נָתַן (to give).

s.line: for I will roll this head all about the room until he promises to give us what we desire.
s.note: גִּלְגֵּל (to roll) is a pi'el with a doubled root, ג־ל־ג־ל, from גַּלְגַּל (wheel). הִתְגַּלְגֵּל = to roll (by itself), and figuratively "to develop, turn out": אֵיךְ הַדְּבָרִים הִתְגַּלְגְּלוּ?

s.line: So be of good cheer, my friends, for all will yet be well.”
s.note: הַכֹּל יִהְיֶה בְּסֵדֶר = "everything will be OK", maybe the most common comforting phrase in Israel. בְּסֵדֶר (literally "in order") = OK, fine. תִּדְאֲגוּ is the plural (to several friends); to one man, אַל תִּדְאַג.

s.line: The next morning the soldier with the green whiskers led the Lion to the great Throne Room and bade him enter the presence of Oz.
s.note: אָמַר לוֹ לְ… + infinitive = "told him to …". הוֹפִיעַ (hif'il) = to appear, show up; הוֹפָעָה = a performance or a show: הָלַכְנוּ לְהוֹפָעָה = we went to a concert. לְהִכָּנֵס is the nif'al infinitive of נִכְנַס.

s.line: The Lion at once passed through the door, and glancing around saw, to his surprise, that before the throne was a Ball of Fire,
s.note: נִמְצָא, the nif'al of מָצָא (to find), literally "is found", but in practice it means "is located, is (there)": אֵיפֹה נִמְצָא הַבַּנְק? = where is the bank? לְהַפְתָּעָתוֹ = to his surprise; לְצַעֲרִי = unfortunately (to my sorrow).

s.line: so fierce and glowing he could scarcely bear to gaze upon it.
s.note: הִצְלִיחַ לְ… + infinitive = "managed to …"; on its own, הִצְלִיחַ = to succeed, and בְּהַצְלָחָה! = good luck! עָצְמָה = intensity, power; מַעֲצָמָה is a world power in the news.

s.line: His first thought was that Oz had by accident caught on fire and was burning up;
s.note: Two pa'al/nif'al pairs: דָּלַק = to be burning / נִדְלַק = to catch fire, light up (הָאוֹר נִדְלַק = the light came on), and שָׂרַף = to burn something / נִשְׂרַף = to be burned, burn up. בְּטָעוּת = by mistake.

s.line: but when he tried to go nearer, the heat was so intense that it singed his whiskers,
s.note: הִתְקָרֵב (hitpa'el) = to come closer, from קָרוֹב (near). The opposite is הִתְרַחֵק (to move away), from רָחוֹק. A cat's or lion's whiskers are שְׂפָמִים; a man's mustache is שָׂפָם.

s.line: and he crept back tremblingly to a spot nearer the door.
s.note: אֲחוֹרָה = backward, with the direction ending ָה (like הַבַּיְתָה); forward is קָדִימָה, also the word for "come on!, let's go!". רוֹעֵד, a participle used like an adverb: "trembling".

w: מִכַּדּוּר הָאֵשׁ|from the Ball of Fire
s.line: Then a low, quiet voice came from the Ball of Fire, and these were the words it spoke:

w: אוֹז הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא|Oz the Great and Terrible
s.line: “I am Oz, the Great and Terrible.
Who are you, and why do you seek me?”
And the Lion answered, “I am a Cowardly Lion, afraid of everything.
s.note: פָּחַד מִ־ = to be afraid of: הוּא פּוֹחֵד מִכְּלָבִים. The ending ָן in פַּחְדָּן marks someone with a habit or trait: שַׁקְרָן liar, בַּיְשָׁן shy person.

s.line: I came to you to beg that you give me courage, so that in reality I may become the King of Beasts, as men call me.”
s.note: קָרָא לְ־ = to call (name) someone: קוֹרְאִים לִי דָּנִי = my name is Danny ("they call me Danny"), the everyday way to give your name. מֶלֶךְ הַחַיּוֹת is the usual Hebrew title of the lion.

w: דָּרַשׁ לָדַעַת|demanded|~idiom: lit. demanded to know
s.line: “Why should I give you courage?” demanded Oz.
“Because of all Wizards you are the greatest, and alone have power to grant my request,” answered the Lion.
s.note: יֵשׁ לְךָ אֶת הַכֹּחַ: with a definite noun, spoken Hebrew puts אֶת after יֵשׁ, as if יֵשׁ were a verb (יֵשׁ לִי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר = I have the book). Strict grammar books object, but you will hear it constantly.

s.line: The Ball of Fire burned fiercely for a time, and the voice said,
s.note: זְמַן מָה = "a while, some time"; מָה after a noun means "some, a certain": לִפְנֵי זְמַן מָה = a while ago.

s.line: “Bring me proof that the Wicked Witch is dead, and that moment I will give you courage.
s.note: תָּבִיא is the future ("you will bring") used as a command, which is how most Israelis give orders in speech; the formal imperative is הָבֵא. הוֹכָחָה = proof; הוֹכִיחַ (hif'il) = to prove.

s.line: But as long as the Witch lives, you must remain a coward.”
s.note: Without vowels, חיה can be חַיָּה (alive, feminine; or "an animal") or חָיָה (he lived). Here it is חַיָּה = alive. חַיָּב = must, obliged; also "owes": אַתָּה חַיָּב לִי כֶּסֶף.

s.line: The Lion was angry at this speech, but could say nothing in reply,
s.note: כָּעַס עַל = to be angry at/about; כַּעַס = anger. יָכֹל here is the past ("could"), spelled like the present יָכוֹל but pointed יָכֹל.

w: בְּכַדּוּר הָאֵשׁ|at the Ball of Fire
וְנָס עַל נַפְשׁוֹ|and fled for his life|~idiom
s.line: and while he stood silently gazing at the Ball of Fire it became so furiously hot that he turned tail and rushed from the room.
s.note: נָס עַל נַפְשׁוֹ = "fled for his life", a set phrase from נָס (to flee); in the news, הַתּוֹשָׁבִים נָסוּ עַל נַפְשָׁם. נַעֲשָׂה (nif'al of עָשָׂה) = to become: נַעֲשָׂה קַר = it got cold. הִסְתּוֹבֵב = to turn around; in the hitpa'el the ת and ס swap.

s.line: He was glad to find his friends waiting for him, and told them of his terrible interview with the Wizard.
s.note: Baum's "interview" meant a formal meeting. Today רֵאָיוֹן is an interview for a job or in the media, so this translation says פְּגִישָׁה (a meeting). שָׂמַח = to be glad; שָׂמֵחַ = glad.

s.line: “What shall we do now?” asked Dorothy sadly.
s.note: מָה נַעֲשֶׂה? = "what shall we do?", the future used for "shall": מָה נַעֲשֶׂה עַכְשָׁיו? is a very common cry of helplessness.

s.line: “There is only one thing we can do,” returned the Lion,
s.note: הֵשִׁיב (hif'il of שׁ־ו־ב, literally "brought back") = to reply, a written alternative to עָנָה. תְּשׁוּבָה (answer) comes from the same root; so does חָזַר בִּתְשׁוּבָה = became religious.

s.line: “and that is to go to the land of the Winkies, seek out the Wicked Witch, and destroy her.”
s.note: הִשְׁמִיד (hif'il) = to destroy, wipe out; הַשְׁמָדָה = destruction. It is a strong, serious word, used in the news for weapons and wars.

s.line: “But suppose we cannot?” said the girl.
s.note: וּמָה אִם…? = "and what if …?", followed by the future: מָה אִם יֵרֵד גֶּשֶׁם? = what if it rains? נוּכַל is the "we" future of יָכוֹל.

w: יִהְיֶה לִי|I will have|~lit. there will be to me
s.line: “Then I shall never have courage,” declared the Lion.
s.note: הִכְרִיז (hif'il) = to declare, announce; הַכְרָזָה = an announcement, a declaration (הַכְרָזַת הָעַצְמָאוּת = the Declaration of Independence). A כָּרוֹז is a public notice or a herald.

w: יִהְיֶה|will have|~lit. there will be (to me)
s.line: “And I shall never have brains,” added the Scarecrow.
s.note: וְלִי comes first because "I" is the new topic: "and as for me, …". הוֹסִיף = to add; נוֹסָף = additional, בְּנוֹסָף = in addition.

w: יִהְיֶה|will have|~lit. there will be (to me)
s.line: “And I shall never have a heart,” spoke the Tin Woodman.
“And I shall never see Aunt Em and Uncle Henry,” said Dorothy, beginning to cry.
s.note: פָּרַץ בִּבְכִי = to burst into tears; also פָּרַץ בִּצְחוֹק = burst out laughing. פָּרַץ alone = to break out or break in: פָּרְצָה שְׂרֵפָה = a fire broke out, פָּרְצוּ לַבַּיִת = they broke into the house.

s.line: “Be careful!” cried the green girl.
s.note: זְהִירוּת! = "careful!, watch out!", the noun used as a warning; you'll see it on signs: זְהִירוּת, מַדְרֵגָה = mind the step. תִּזָּהֵר! (to a man) / תִּזָּהֲרִי! (to a woman) are the verb forms.

s.line: “The tears will fall on your green silk gown and spot it.”
s.note: שִׂמְלַת הַמֶּשִׁי הַיְּרֻקָּה: in a construct pair the adjective comes after the whole pair and agrees with the first noun, so הַיְּרֻקָּה (feminine) goes with שִׂמְלָה, not with מֶשִׁי. כֶּתֶם = a stain, spot.

s.line: So Dorothy dried her eyes and said, “I suppose we must try it;
s.note: הִנִּיחַ (hif'il) = to put down, and also "to assume, suppose": אֲנִי מַנִּיחַ שֶׁהוּא יָבוֹא = I assume he'll come. הַנָּחָה = an assumption (and also a discount!). נִגֵּב = to wipe dry; מַגֶּבֶת = a towel.

s.line: but I am sure I do not want to kill anybody, even to see Aunt Em again.”
“I will go with you; but I’m too much of a coward to kill the Witch,” said the Lion.
s.note: מִדַּי = too (much): חַם מִדַּי = too hot, יָקָר מִדַּי = too expensive. "Too … to …" is מִדַּי + בִּשְׁבִיל / כְּדֵי + infinitive.

s.line: “I will go too,” declared the Scarecrow;
“but I shall not be of much help to you, I am such a fool.”
s.note: הָיָה לְעֶזְרָה = to be of help: אִם אוּכַל לִהְיוֹת לְעֶזְרָה… = if I can be of help…. הָיָה לְ־ + noun often means "to serve as, become".

w: אֵין לִי|I haven't|~lit. there isn't to me
s.line: “I haven’t the heart to harm even a Witch,” remarked the Tin Woodman;
s.note: Baum makes a joke here: "I haven't the heart to …" means "I can't bring myself to …", and the Tin Woodman really has no heart. The Hebrew keeps the literal words. פָּגַע בְּ־ = to hurt, harm (with בְּ); נִפְגַּע = was hurt, and פִּגּוּעַ = a terror attack in the news.

s.line: “but if you go I certainly shall go with you.”
s.note: בְּוַדַּאי = certainly, of course; בְּוַדַּאי שֶׁ… = "of course …". וַדַּאי = certain; in speech you will also hear בָּטוּחַ and בֶּטַח (sure!).

w: לָצֵאת לַדֶּרֶךְ|to set out|~idiom: lit. to go out to the road
s.line: Therefore it was decided to start upon their journey the next morning,
s.note: הֻחְלַט is the hof'al (passive) of הֶחְלִיט (to decide): הֵם הֶחְלִיטוּ → הֻחְלַט = it was decided. You'll meet it in the news: הֻחְלַט לִסְגֹּר אֶת בֵּית הַסֵּפֶר. יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ = to set out; דֶּרֶךְ צְלֵחָה! = have a good trip!

w: אֶבֶן מַשְׁחֶזֶת|a grindstone|~lit. a sharpening stone
s.line: and the Woodman sharpened his axe on a green grindstone and had all his joints properly oiled.
s.note: דָּאַג שֶׁ… = "made sure that, saw to it that", the Hebrew for English "had (something) done": דָּאַגְתִּי שֶׁיְּתַקְּנוּ אֶת הַמְּכוֹנִית = I had the car fixed. דָּאַג לְ־ = to take care of; דָּאַג alone = to worry.

s.line: The Scarecrow stuffed himself with fresh straw and Dorothy put new paint on his eyes that he might see better.
s.note: אֶת עַצְמוֹ = himself, as the object of a verb: הוּא מִלֵּא אֶת עַצְמוֹ. מֵחָדָשׁ = again, anew (from חָדָשׁ, new): לְהַתְחִיל מֵחָדָשׁ = to start over.

s.line: The green girl, who was very kind to them, filled Dorothy’s basket with good things to eat,
s.note: נֶחְמָד אֶל / לְ־ = nice to someone; נֶחְמָד is one of the most used adjectives in Hebrew ("nice, pleasant"). מִלֵּא אֶת X בְּ־ = filled X with …: the container is the object and the contents take בְּ.

s.line: and fastened a little bell around Toto’s neck with a green ribbon.
s.note: סֶרֶט = a ribbon, but today it mostly means a film: הָלַכְנוּ לִרְאוֹת סֶרֶט = we went to see a movie (a film was originally a strip of celluloid). קָשַׁר = to tie; קֶשֶׁר = a knot, and also a connection.

s.line: They went to bed quite early and slept soundly until daylight,
s.note: לְמַדַּי = "quite, fairly", placed after the word: טוֹב לְמַדַּי = good enough, fairly good. Compare מִדַּי = too. יָשַׁן שֵׁנָה עֲמֻקָּה = slept a deep sleep, the verb + noun from one root.

s.line: when they were awakened by the crowing of a green cock that lived in the back yard of the Palace, and the cackling of a hen that had laid a green egg.
s.note: הִתְעוֹרֵר (hitpa'el) = to wake up; הֵעִיר (hif'il) = to wake someone up, שָׁעוֹן מְעוֹרֵר = alarm clock. הֵטִיל בֵּיצָה = laid an egg; in the news הֵטִיל = to impose: הֵטִילוּ מַס = they imposed a tax.
